title: How Votes Become Seats
hook: The same ballots can produce very different results depending on the electoral system used to count them.
key_points: An electoral system is the set of rules turning votes into seats or offices.
Plurality ('first-past-the-post'): the candidate with the most votes in a district wins.
Proportional representation: seats are allocated roughly in proportion to each party's vote share.
Each system trades off simplicity, local representation, and how closely seats mirror votes.
content_html: An electoral system is the set of rules that converts the votes people cast into seats in a legislature or into who holds an office. It is easy to overlook, but the choice of system shapes outcomes profoundly — the very same set of ballots can hand victory to different parties depending on the counting rules.
extra_html: Two broad families illustrate the range. Under plurality systems — often called "first-past-the-post" — a country is divided into districts and whoever wins the most votes in each district takes the seat, even without an outright majority. This is simple and gives each area a clear local representative, but a party's share of seats can diverge sharply from its share of votes. Proportional representation instead allocates seats to match each party's overall vote share, so a party winning a quarter of the vote earns roughly a quarter of the seats; this mirrors public opinion more closely but can produce many parties and coalition governments. Other systems, such as ranked-choice and mixed-member designs, blend these goals. Encyclopaedia Britannica surveys how elections function and the trade-offs each system makes; none is objectively "best" — each balances simplicity, local ties, and proportionality differently.

flashcards.prompt: What does an electoral system do?
flashcards.back_html: It defines the rules for turning votes into seats or offices — different rules can yield different winners from the same ballots.

flashcards.prompt: How does 'first-past-the-post' (plurality) decide a district's winner?

choices.text: The candidate with the most votes wins, even without a majority
Seats are split in proportion to each party's vote share
The candidate with the fewest votes wins

flashcards.explanation_html: Under plurality, whoever gets the most votes in the district wins — a majority isn't required.

flashcards.prompt: What does proportional representation aim to do?

choices.text: Allocate seats roughly in proportion to each party's share of the vote
Give every seat to the single most popular party
Eliminate the need to count votes

flashcards.explanation_html: PR tries to match each party's seat count to its vote share, so smaller parties can win representation.
